downsample.text:
# tsdownsample [![PyPI Latest Release](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/tsdownsample.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/tsdownsample/) [![support-version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/tsdownsample)](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/tsdownsample) [![Downloads](https://static.pepy.tech/badge/tsdownsample)](https://pepy.tech/project/tsdownsample) [![CodeQL](https://github.com/predict-idlab/tsdownsample/actions/workflows/codeql.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/predict-idlab/tsdownsample/actions/workflows/codeql.yml) [![Testing](https://github.com/predict-idlab/tsdownsample/actions/workflows/ci-downsample_rs.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/predict-idlab/tsdownsample/actions/workflows/ci-downsample_rs.yml) [![Testing](https://github.com/predict-idlab/tsdownsample/actions/workflows/ci-tsdownsample.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/predict-idlab/tsdownsample/actions/workflows/ci-tsdownsample.yml) [![Discord](https://img.shields.io/badge/Discord-%235865F2.svg?logo=discord&logoColor=white)](https://discord.gg/k2d59GrxPX) Extremely fast **time series downsampling 📈** for visualization, written in Rust. ## Features ✨ - **Fast**: written in rust with PyO3 bindings - leverages optimized [argminmax](https://github.com/jvdd/argminmax) - which is SIMD accelerated with runtime feature detection - scales linearly with the number of data points - multithreaded with Rayon (in Rust)
Why we do not use Python multiprocessing Citing the PyO3 docs on parallelism:
CPython has the infamous Global Interpreter Lock, which prevents several threads from executing Python bytecode in parallel. This makes threading in Python a bad fit for CPU-bound tasks and often forces developers to accept the overhead of multiprocessing.
In Rust - which is a compiled language - there is no GIL, so CPU-bound tasks can be parallelized (with Rayon) with little to no overhead.
- **Efficient**: memory efficient - works on views of the data (no copies) - no intermediate data structures are created - **Flexible**: works on any type of data - supported datatypes are - for `x`: `f32`, `f64`, `i16`, `i32`, `i64`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`, `datetime64`, `timedelta64` - for `y`: `f16`, `f32`, `f64`, `i8`, `i16`, `i32`, `i64`, `u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`, `datetime64`, `timedelta64`, `bool`
!! 🚀 f16 argminmax is 200-300x faster than numpy In contrast with all other data types above, f16 is *not* hardware supported (i.e., no instructions for f16) by most modern CPUs!!
🐌 Programming languages facilitate support for this datatype by either (i) upcasting to f32 or (ii) using a software implementation.
💡 As for argminmax, only comparisons are needed - and thus no arithmetic operations - creating a symmetrical ordinal mapping from f16 to i16 is sufficient. This mapping allows to use the hardware supported scalar and SIMD i16 instructions - while not producing any memory overhead 🎉
More details are described in argminmax PR #1.
- **Easy to use**: simple & flexible API ## Install ```bash pip install tsdownsample ``` ## Usage ```python from tsdownsample import MinMaxLTTBDownsampler import numpy as np # Create a time series y = np.random.randn(10_000_000) x = np.arange(len(y)) # Downsample to 1000 points (assuming constant sampling rate) s_ds = MinMaxLTTBDownsampler().downsample(y, n_out=1000) # Select downsampled data downsampled_y = y[s_ds] # Downsample to 1000 points using the (possible irregularly spaced) x-data s_ds = MinMaxLTTBDownsampler().downsample(x, y, n_out=1000) # Select downsampled data downsampled_x = x[s_ds] downsampled_y = y[s_ds] ``` ## Downsampling algorithms & API ### Downsampling API 📑 Each downsampling algorithm is implemented as a class that implements a `downsample` method. The signature of the `downsample` method: ``` downsample([x], y, n_out, **kwargs) -> ndarray[uint64] ``` **Arguments**: - `x` is optional - `x` and `y` are both positional arguments - `n_out` is a mandatory keyword argument that defines the number of output values* - `**kwargs` are optional keyword arguments *(see [table below](#downsampling-algorithms-📈))*: - `parallel`: whether to use multi-threading (default: `False`) ❗ The max number of threads can be configured with the `TSDOWNSAMPLE_MAX_THREADS` ENV var (e.g. `os.environ["TSDOWNSAMPLE_MAX_THREADS"] = "4"`) - ... **Returns**: a `ndarray[uint64]` of indices that can be used to index the original data. \*When there are gaps in the time series, fewer than `n_out` indices may be returned. ### Downsampling algorithms 📈 The following downsampling algorithms (classes) are implemented: | Downsampler | Description | `**kwargs` | | ---:| --- |--- | | `MinMaxDownsampler` | selects the **min and max** value in each bin | `parallel` | | `M4Downsampler` | selects the [**min, max, first and last**](https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.14778/2732951.2732953) value in each bin | `parallel` | | `LTTBDownsampler` | performs the [**Largest Triangle Three Buckets**](https://skemman.is/bitstream/1946/15343/3/SS_MSthesis.pdf) algorithm | `parallel` | | `MinMaxLTTBDownsampler` | (*new two-step algorithm 🎉*) first selects `n_out` * `minmax_ratio` **min and max** values, then further reduces these to `n_out` values using the **Largest Triangle Three Buckets** algorithm | `parallel`, `minmax_ratio`* | *Default value for `minmax_ratio` is 4, which is empirically proven to be a good default. More details here: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.00332 ### Handling NaNs This library supports two `NaN`-policies: 1. Omit `NaN`s (`NaN`s are ignored during downsampling). 2. Return index of first `NaN` once there is at least one present in the bin of the considered data. | Omit `NaN`s | Return `NaN`s | | ----------------------: | :------------------------- | | `MinMaxDownsampler` | `NaNMinMaxDownsampler` | | `M4Downsampler` | `NaNM4Downsampler` | | `MinMaxLTTBDownsampler` | `NaNMinMaxLTTBDownsampler` | | `LTTBDownsampler` | | > Note that NaNs are not supported for `x`-data. ## Limitations & assumptions 🚨 Assumes; 1. `x`-data is (non-strictly) monotonic increasing (i.e., sorted) 2. no `NaN`s in `x`-data ---

👤 Jeroen Van Der Donckt

[package]
name = "py-autosar-data"
version = "0.17.0"
edition = "2024"
description = "read, write and modify Autosar arxml data using Python"
authors = ["Daniel Thaler <daniel@dthaler.de>"]
license = "MIT OR Apache-2.0"
keywords = ["arxml", "automotive", "file-format", "Autosar"]

[lib]
name = "_autosar_data"
crate-type = ["cdylib"]

[dependencies]
autosar-data = "0.23"
autosar-data-specification = "0.23"
autosar-data-abstraction = "0.11.2"
pyo3 = "0.29"

CANoe AI Features

Accelerate Engineering Workflows in CANoe With AI and MCP
Try It Now

Turn complex engineering tasks into simple prompts. The CANoe AI features support you to analyze configurations, investigate logs, create CAPL code, and automate complete testing workflows using natural language. AI agents autonomously execute tasks in CANoe, identify relevant findings, and guide you to the next steps. This reduces manual effort, shortens development cycles, and enables both experienced CANoe users and newcomers to work more efficiently.

You continue to use your existing LLM, such as the one behind GitHub Copilot or Claude, while Vector provides the AI layer consisting of agents, skills, and MCP tools.

Your Benefits

  • Complete your engineering tasks faster by turning manual multi-step workflows into AI-assisted processes driven by natural language.
  • Reduce routine work with AI agents that automatically generate, execute, analyze, and refine test scenarios.
  • Find issues more quickly through intelligent analysis of logs, reports, network traffic, and CANoe configurations.
  • Increase productivity at every user level by making advanced CANoe functionality reachable through simple prompts.
  • Stay in control of your data and workflows with transparent AI interactions and the freedom to use your preferred AI endpoint.

How It Works

Bring the AI you already use to the CANoe Agentic Ecosystem.

Getting started is simple. 

You bring your endpoint — the same one behind your GitHub Copilot, Claude, or in-house LLM. Use it from VS Code, the Vector chat client, or any IDE with a compatible MCP client. The connection to the CANoe MCP Server happens automatically.

Vector provides the agentic ecosystem. 

The Discovery, Project, Simulation, Coding, and Analysis Agents work with skills and MCP tools. Behind them is the Vector RAG. It grounds the agents in Vector's knowledge base and documentation, so answers rely on Vector's expertise rather than guesswork of the model. The ecosystem remains open, allowing you to bring in your own agents, skills, MCP tools, and context to tailor it to your needs.

Download the CANoe AI Package
To make CANoe promptable, install the CANoe AI Package. This downloadable bundle provides a collection of AI skills and agents that teach AI coding tools to work with CANoe. These assets supply the necessary domain-specific knowledge, allowing AI agents to effectively use the CANoe MCP Server and CANoe Documentation MCP Server. Once integrated into your preferred AI tool, the skills and agents work seamlessly with the MCP servers.
More About the CANoe AI Package

Your Feedback

Your feedback helps us shape the future of AI-assisted workflows in CANoe. We would like to know your feedback on the new AI and MCP features. Let us know what works well for your use cases, where you see room for improvement, and which capabilities you would like to see in future releases.

Open the Feedback Form

From Requirement to Reviewed Results

Using the CANoe Agentic Ecosystem, you can accelerate your workflows. After receiving a new requirement, an agent turns it into CAPL test code, executes it in CANoe, analyzes any failures, repairs the code, and reruns the test. When the workflow is complete, it hands you the exact scenario to review, with the relevant CANoe windows already synchronized.

Describe Your Task – The Agents Handle The Implementation

You choose how much you hand over — from a single question to a fully orchestrated run, and everything in between. The agents work out which capabilities the task needs and chain them for you.

The examples in the following videos are using VS Code, GitHub Copilot, and CANoe.

Build CANoe Simulations in Minutes

Speed up Your Testing Processes

Analyzing Communication Issues Faster

From Test Specification to Test Implementation

Human in the Loop: The Agents Work and You Decide

Autonomy doesn't mean being out of sight. Every run is transparent, and every result is delivered to you. You always have the choice of how much to delegate.

Every step is visible

You see live, which MCP tools the agent calls, which skills it uses, and what it changes in your IDE and in CANoe.

Results come to you

The agents analyze and report back with concrete next steps and CANoe views synchronized to what matters. They are prepared for your judgment, not instead of it.

You set the depth

Ask, act, delegate, or orchestrate — the same system serves all four purposes. Move along the scale whenever you choose.

Wondering What's Possible With Your Configuration? The Discovery Agent Will Tell You

Your setup — your buses, your ECUs, your code — opens its own possibilities. Load your configuration and let the Discovery Agent explore them with you. It reads what's there, knows which agents and skills are at hand, and derives what you could do with them

Use Our Agents, Adapt Them, or Build Your Own.

The agents and skills we provide are just starting points. Adjust them to your workflows or write your own agents using the same tools. We enable you to bring this into your workflow. Get in touch and discuss your use cases with us.

Product Management CANoe AI Features
Get in Touch
We are happy to answer your questions, provide further information, and discuss your use cases and workflows. Together, we will find a solution, how agents, skills, and MCP tools map to your needs.

Your Next Steps

Try It Today!

The CANoe MCP Server is available now in CANoe 20 SP 2. Connect your MCP client, load a configuration, and send your first prompt.

Learn More About CANoe

CANoe is Vector's versatile tool for developing, simulating, analyzing and testing individual software components, subsystems, electronic control units (ECUs), and entire distributed networks.

We build the intelligent foundation teams need to develop and operate the software-defined systems of tomorrow.
